newsitem.title: USA: USDA suspends new salvage rider timber sales.
newsitem.headline: USDA suspends new salvage rider timber sales.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department confirmed Friday it was suspending new sales of timber from national forests under the salvage logging rider.
USDA Undersecretary James Lyons said the Forest Service will halt advertising for timber sales under the emergency salvage rider.
"As of today, no more salvage sales will be advertised under the emergency salvage timber program," Lyons said in a telephone interview.

Lyons said advertising for new sales was being stopped to "provide for an orderly transition between the emergency program and our normal sales program" as the emergency salvage rider expires December 31.

He also said, "There's been a lot of public criticism of the program and some were fostering this perception that there was going to be some kind of Christmas rush to get sales out. Well this should allay peoples' fears about the Christmas rush."
Lyons said he did not know the volume of timber that would be affected by the suspension, but the American Forest and Paper Association estimated it would affect about 100 million board feet.

As of November 30, the Forest Service has offered 4.1 billion board feet under the emergency salvage rider. Lyons said that was about 90 percent of the goal "that we had to agree to with the Congress."

The emergency salvage rider which Congress passed in 1995 was to expedite logging of dead and dying trees in national forests by reducing or eliminating many environmental reviews and opportunities for public comment and opposition.
The timber industry said it was needed to remove a dangerous fuel build-up in the national forests, but environmentalists said it was intended to give the timber industry more access to trees.
